title: With the Childlike People

teacherSummary.text: Siddhartha works for Kamaswami but treats business as a game, caring little for profit, which irritates the merchant yet makes Siddhartha successful. He watches ordinary people—the 'childlike people'—with amusement as they suffer over money and desire. Kamala teaches him the art of love, and they agree that neither of them can truly love.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “With the Childlike People,” how does Hesse show detachment among the childlike people? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how With the Childlike People develops the idea of detachment among the childlike people. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and irony shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses characterization in With the Childlike People to complicate the reader's understanding of detachment among the childlike people. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate With the Childlike People within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of detachment among the childlike people responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads With the Childlike People as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of detachment among the childlike people. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

satQuestions.passage: “It is very good, sir. When a person has nothing to eat, fasting is the smartest thing he could do. segments.activity: Quick-write and share on the opening question.
segments.script: Good morning, readers. Before we open the book, take three minutes and write your honest answer to this: Siddhartha calls others 'childlike.' Is he being wise or arrogant? There is no wrong answer yet; we will test our ideas against the text today.

segments.activity: Model pronouncing, defining and using five key words in context.
segments.script: Today's words include businesses, storage, bananas, hastiness, besiege. Watch how I figure out a word from its sentence before I check the dictionary. Here is the line: “Besides from this, Siddhartha’s interest and curiosity was only concerned with the people, whose businesses, crafts, worries, pleasures, and acts of foolishness used to be as alien and distant to him as the moon.” My guess comes from the clues around it; the dictionary says: That which busies one, or that which engages the time, attention, or labor of any one, as his principal concern or….

segments.activity: Present background, then the significance of the chapter.
segments.script: Let me give you some background that the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Hesse contrasts spiritual detachment with worldly attachment, echoing Buddhist teaching on desire. Now, why does this chapter matter? Siddhartha's superiority is ironic: he is beginning to become what he looks down on. As you listen, jot one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Irony, Theme.
segments.script: Let's read this passage together. I will read the first sentence; you track along. Every time you spot characterization, mark it. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice here? I will collect three ideas on the board and we will choose the strongest one together, using the evidence.
